lessons.title: Pre-Operation Checks and Daily Maintenance
lessons.body: Before you start any small Chinese machineâwhether it's a diesel water pump, a maize mill, or a block-making machineâyou must do a daily check. This takes 10 minutes and prevents 80% of breakdowns. First, look at the machine. Check for loose bolts, cracks in the frame, or oil leaks on the ground. A small leak today becomes a seized engine tomorrow. Next, check the fuel level. For diesel engines, fill the tank at least half full to avoid condensation. Use a clean funnel with a fine mesh filterâdirty fuel is the number one killer of Chinese injector pumps. Check the air filter: if it's clogged with dust, tap it gently or wash it in soapy water (if it's a foam filter) and let it dry completely before reinstalling. Never run an engine without an air filter. Check the oil level with the dipstick. The oil should be between the two marks. If it's black and thick, change it. For most small Chinese diesels, use SAE 15W-40 or 20W-50 depending on your climate. In hot African conditions, 20W-50 is often better. Also check the cooling system: for water-cooled engines, ensure the radiator is full and the fan belt has about 1 cm of play. For air-cooled engines, clean the cooling fins with a brush. Finally, do a quick start test: listen for unusual noises, check for smoke (black smoke means too much fuel or a dirty air filter; white smoke means water in fuel or low compression). After running for 2 minutes, switch off and re-check for leaks. Record everything in a small notebookâdate, hours run, and any issues. This habit will save you money and downtime.

lessons.title: Safe Operating Procedures for Key Machines
lessons.body: Every machine has its own safe operating procedure, but some rules apply to all. First, never wear loose clothing, jewellery, or open shoes. Tie back long hair. Wear safety glasses when using grinders or chippers, and ear muffs when running a maize mill or generator for more than 30 minutes. For a diesel generator: start it with no load, let it warm up for 2 minutes, then switch on appliances one by one. Never overload itâif the breaker trips, reduce the load. For a water pump: prime it before starting (fill the pump casing with water), then start the engine and slowly open the discharge valve. Running dry will destroy the seal in minutes. For a maize mill: feed grain slowly and evenly. If the mill jams, switch off immediately, wait for the engine to stop, then clear the blockage with a wooden stickânever your hand. For a block-making machine: keep hands clear of the mould and ram. Use a push stick to remove finished blocks. Always switch off and disconnect the spark plug or battery before doing any maintenance. When operating a welding machine, ensure good ventilation, wear a welding helmet, and keep a fire extinguisher nearby. Never leave a running machine unattended. If you must step away, switch it off. In Africa, many accidents happen because someone left a machine running while they went to greet a neighbour. Also, keep children and animals away from the work area. Use barriers or a simple rope. Finally, know your emergency stop: most Chinese machines have a red button or a kill switch. Test it weekly. If it doesn't work, fix it before using the machine.

lessons.title: Preventing Common Accidents
lessons.body: Most accidents with small machines are predictable and preventable. The top five are: cuts from blades, burns from hot engines, electric shocks, fuel fires, and crushed fingers. Let's tackle each. Cuts: always use sharp blades. A dull blade requires more force and slips. When changing a blade on a circular saw or chipper, wear cut-resistant gloves and use a spanner, not your hand. Keep blades covered when not in use. Burns: exhaust pipes and engine blocks get hotter than boiling water. Let the machine cool for 15 minutes before touching. Use a rag or gloves. Never open a radiator cap while the engine is hotâsteam will scald you. Electric shocks: check cables for cracks. Use an RCD (residual current device) if you have mains power. For generators, ensure the frame is earthed with a copper rod. Never run a generator in a wet area. Fuel fires: store fuel in a proper jerry can, not a plastic bottle. Refuel only when the engine is off and cool. Keep a dry powder fire extinguisher within 3 metres of the machine. If a fire starts, switch off the fuel valve and use the extinguisherânever water on a fuel fire. Crushed fingers: use push sticks, jigs, and clamps. Never put your hand near moving parts. For block machines, keep the guard in place. Also, prevent slips and trips: clean up oil spills immediately with sand or sawdust. Keep tools organised. In many African workshops, accidents happen because of poor lighting. Install a simple LED floodlight. Finally, have a first aid kit with bandages, antiseptic, and burn gel. Train everyone on basic first aid. If an accident happens, stop the machine first, then help the injured person.

lessons.title: Fuel and Lubricant Management
lessons.body: Fuel and lubricants are the lifeblood of your machine. Poor management leads to costly repairs. Start with fuel storage. Buy diesel or petrol in clean, labelled jerry cans. Store them in a cool, ventilated place away from direct sunlight and ignition sources. Never store fuel in open buckets or plastic bottlesâthey can melt or static-spark. For diesel, let it settle for 24 hours before use so water and dirt sink to the bottom. Then decant the top 90% through a fine filter (5 microns). Add a fuel additive if you have water problemsâa common issue in humid African climates. For petrol, use fresh fuel; stale petrol (older than 3 months) gums up carburettors. Always use the correct fuel: diesel engines need diesel, not kerosene or petrol. Mixing fuels will destroy the injector pump. For lubricants: use the oil grade recommended in the manual. If you don't have a manual, use SAE 15W-40 for most small diesels, and SAE 30 for petrol engines in warm climates. Change engine oil every 100 hours of operation or every 3 months, whichever comes first. Change the oil filter at the same time. For gearboxes and hydraulic systems, use the specified gear oil (often 80W-90) and check levels weekly. Grease all nipples every 50 hours with lithium grease. Keep a logbook: date, hours, oil added, and next service. Buy lubricants in sealed containers from a reputable dealerâfake oil is common and will ruin your engine. If you must store oil, keep it clean and labelled. Never mix different oils. Finally, dispose of used oil properly: collect it in a drum and sell it to a recycler, or take it to a garage. Never pour it on the ground or into riversâit poisons water and soil.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Minor Breakdowns
lessons.body: When your machine stops working, don't panic. Most problems are simple. Start with the basics: fuel, air, spark, compression. For a diesel engine that won't start: check fuel valve is open, fuel filter is not clogged, and there is no air in the fuel line (bleed the injector lines). If it starts then dies, the fuel cap vent may be blockedâloosen it. If it runs rough, check the air filter and injector. For a petrol engine: check spark plugâclean it with a wire brush, set gap to 0.7-0.8 mm, or replace it. Check fuel flow to carburettor. If the engine surges, clean the carburettor with carb cleaner. For a water pump that loses prime: check suction hose for leaks, ensure foot valve is not stuck, and that the pump casing is full of water. For a maize mill that vibrates: check for worn hammers or unbalanced pulley. Tighten all bolts. For a block machine that jams: switch off, clear debris, and check for worn bearings. For electrical problems: check fuses, loose wires, and brushes on motors. Use a multimeter to test continuity. If a belt squeals, tighten it or replace it. If a bearing rumbles, replace itâdon't wait. Always use the right tools: spanners, screwdrivers, and a hammer. Keep a basic tool kit with the machine. If you can't fix it in 30 minutes, stop and call a professional. Many people make it worse by forcing parts. Also, keep spare parts: fuel filters, air filters, spark plugs, belts, and fuses. In rural Africa, waiting for a part can take days. So stock common spares. Finally, after any repair, run the machine for 5 minutes and check for leaks and unusual noises.

lessons.title: When to Call a Professional Technician
lessons.body: Knowing when to stop and call a technician is a skill that saves money and lives. You should call a professional if: the problem is inside the engine (e.g., knocking noise, blue smoke, loss of compression), the repair requires special tools (e.g., injector pump timing, hydraulic press), or the machine is under warranty. Also, if you have tried basic troubleshooting and failed, don't keep forcing it. For electrical issues involving the main winding or control panel, call a qualified electrician. For welding cracks in the engine block or cylinder head, call a welder with experience in cast iron. For fuel injection systems, call a diesel mechanicâthey have test benches and calibrated tools. In Africa, many technicians are self-taught, so ask for recommendations from other business owners. Check if they have worked on your brand of Chinese machine (e.g., Changfa, Sifang, Jiangdong). Before they come, note the machine model, serial number, and symptoms. Have the manual ready if you have it. Agree on a price and warranty for the repair. A good technician will diagnose first, explain the problem, and give you a quote. Avoid anyone who wants to open the engine immediately without checking the basics. Also, learn from the technician: watch what they do and ask questions. That way, next time you might fix it yourself. Finally, keep a record of all repairs. If a machine breaks down frequently, it might be cheaper to replace it than to keep repairing. A small Chinese diesel engine typically lasts 5,000-8,000 hours with good maintenance. If yours has done 10,000 hours and is costing you money every month, consider buying a new one.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Machine Operation and Safety for Small Chinese Machines in African Agribusiness

Small Chinese machines â from 2â8 hp diesel water pumps and tillers to maize shellers, rice threshers, and multi-crop grinders â have become the backbone of smallholder mechanisation across Africa. They are affordable, widely available through importers in Lagos, Nairobi, Accra, and Dar es Salaam, and simple enough for local mechanics to service. But they are also unforgiving: poor fuel, missed lubrication, and shortcut safety practices destroy more of these machines than any manufacturing defect. This practical reference gives you field-tested procedures to keep machines running, workers safe, and money in the business.

Why This Matters to Your Business

A 7 hp diesel engine that fails prematurely costs US$350â600 to replace â often more than the seasonal profit from the hectare it serves. Downtime during harvest or irrigation windows is worse: crops spoil, contracts are lost, and customers move to competitors. The procedures below are designed around three business outcomes: extend machine life, reduce unplanned downtime, and protect the people who operate your equipment.

1. Pre-Operation Checks and Daily Maintenance

Every operator should run a 5-minute check before starting any machine. This is not optional â it is the cheapest insurance you can buy.

Table 1: Daily Pre-Operation Check Schedule for Small Diesel Machines
Check What to Look For Action if Wrong Time
Engine oil Level between MIN and MAX on dipstick; colour honey-brown to dark brown Top up with SAE 30 or 15W-40; if milky or gritty, change oil 60 sec
Fuel Clean diesel, no water or dirt; tank at least half full Drain water trap; refill with filtered diesel 60 sec
Air filter Dry, light-coloured element; no dust caking Tap clean or replace; never run without filter 45 sec
Coolant / cooling fins Air-cooled: fins free of chaff and mud. Water-cooled: level at mark Brush clean; top up coolant 45 sec
Belts and couplings Tension ~10 mm deflection; no cracks or glazing Tighten or replace 45 sec
Fasteners and guards Bolts tight; guards in place; no exposed moving parts Tighten, refit guards before starting 45 sec

Source: Adapted from FAO, "Farm Power and Machinery Management" and Kubota/Yanmar agricultural engine operator manuals distributed with Chinese-brand engines (Dongfeng, Changfa, Jiangdong).

2. Safe Operating Procedures for Key Machines

The three machines most common in African smallholder operations are diesel water pumps, power tillers, and maize/rice threshers. Each has specific hazards.

  • Water pumps: Prime before starting (dry running destroys seals in minutes). Place on level ground. Keep intake strainer clear of mud and debris. Never run the engine in an enclosed shed â carbon monoxide kills silently.
  • Power tillers: Engage clutch slowly; never stand in front of the tiller. Keep hands on handles, not on the engine. On slopes, work across the contour, not up and down.
  • Threshers and shellers: Feed evenly â jamming causes belt slip and injury when clearing. Use a wooden pusher, never your hand. Keep loose clothing, shawls, and jewellery away from belts and pulleys.

3. Preventing Common Accidents

Most accidents with small machines fall into four categories: entanglement, burns, fuel fires, and crushing. Each has a simple prevention.

Table 2: Common Accidents, Causes and Prevention for Small Farm Machines
Accident Type Common Cause Prevention First Response
Entanglement Loose clothing, shawls, long hair near belts/pulleys Fit guards; tie back hair; no loose clothing Stop engine immediately; do not pull victim
Burns Touching hot exhaust or muffler after shutdown Fit heat shield; wait 15 min before servicing Cool with clean water; seek clinic if blistered
Fuel fire Refuelling while engine hot or running; spilled fuel on hot surface Shut down and cool 10 min before refuelling; use funnel Smother with sand or COâ; never water on diesel
Crushing / cuts Clearing jams with hands while engine runs Always stop engine and remove key before clearing Apply pressure to bleeding; seek medical help

Source: Compiled from ILO, "Safety and Health in Agriculture" (Code of Practice, 2010), and the African Newsletter on Occupational Health and Safety, Vol. 24 (2014).

â  SAFETY WARNING â CARBON MONOXIDE

Never operate a petrol or diesel engine inside a closed room, grain store, or vehicle. Carbon monoxide is colourless, odourless, and kills within minutes. In 2019, the WHO reported that household and occupational exposure to engine exhaust contributes to over 3.8 million premature deaths annually, with significant burden in sub-Saharan Africa where enclosed engine use is common. Always run engines outdoors or with forced ventilation.

4. Fuel and Lubricant Management

Dirty fuel is the number-one killer of small diesel engines in Africa. Injector pumps and nozzles are machined to tolerances of a few microns; a single teaspoon of grit can destroy them.

  • Buy clean fuel: Use a reputable station, not roadside jerrycans of unknown quality.
  • Filter every fill: A simple funnel with a 5-micron mesh element costs under US$10 and saves hundreds in pump repairs.
  • Store properly: Keep fuel in sealed drums, off the ground, out of direct sun. Use within 3 months â diesel degrades.
  • Water trap: Drain the fuel filter water trap daily; water causes rust and injector tip erosion.
  • Lubricants: Use the grade specified in the manual â typically SAE 30 or 15W-40 for engines, SAE 90 for gearboxes. Cheap "recycled" oil destroys bearings.
  • Grease points: Grease wheel bearings, tiller tine shafts, and thresher pulleys weekly during heavy use.

5. Troubleshooting Minor Breakdowns

Before calling a technician, work through this sequence â most no-start problems are fuel or air related.

  1. Engine won't start: Check fuel tap open, fuel in tank, air filter clean, decompression lever released, and battery charged (if electric start).
  2. Engine starts then dies: Air in fuel line â bleed the system at the filter and injector.
  3. White/blue smoke: Cold engine or over-fuelling; check injector. Black smoke: overloaded or dirty air filter.
  4. Loss of power: Clogged air filter, dirty fuel filter, or worn injector nozzle.
  5. Overheating: Blocked cooling fins, low oil, or continuous overload. Stop and cool before restarting.
  6. Vibration or noise: Loose mounting bolts, damaged pulley, or worn bearing â stop immediately.

6. When to Call a Professional Technician

Some jobs require tools, training, and calibration equipment you do not have. Call a qualified technician when:

  • The engine needs a full strip-down (piston, rings, bearings, crankshaft).
  • Fuel injection pump or injector nozzle requires calibration â this needs a test bench.
  • Electrical system faults (alternator, starter motor, wiring harness) beyond fuse and battery checks.
  • Repeated overheating or knocking after basic checks â indicates internal damage.
  • Any repair that requires welding, machining, or precision measurement.

Build a relationship with a trusted technician before you need one. Ask for references, agree on rates, and keep a simple maintenance log for every machine â this alone extends engine life by 20â30% in field studies.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Check engine oil level and colour before every start.
  2. Drain water trap and inspect fuel filter daily.
  3. Clean air filter every 50 hours; replace when clogged.
  4. Keep all guards fitted and fasteners tight.
  5. Refuel only when engine is off and cool â never while running.
  6. Stop engine and remove key before clearing any jam.
  7. Keep bystanders and children 5 m away from operating machines.
  8. Log every breakdown and repair in a machine notebook.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Farm Power and Machinery Management (free PDF)
  • ILO â Safety and Health in Agriculture: Code of Practice
  • WHO â Household Air Pollution and Health Fact Sheet
  • WHO Africa â Occupational Health Resources
  • AgriSETA (South Africa) â Agricultural Machinery Safety Guides

Prepared as part of the Rise Africa Skills course Small Chinese Machines â Machine Operation and Safety. Adapt figures and fuel grades to the specific manual supplied with your machine.

quiz.q: What is the first thing you should check before starting a small Chinese diesel engine?
options: A) The fuel level and for leaks
B) The colour of the exhaust smoke
C) The air pressure in the tyres
D) The speed of the engine
quiz.explanation: Checking fuel level and leaks prevents fuel starvation and fire hazards.

quiz.q: How often should you change the engine oil in a small Chinese diesel engine under normal conditions?
quiz.explanation: Most manuals recommend oil changes every 100 hours or 3 months, whichever comes first.

quiz.q: What should you do if the air filter is clogged with dust?
options: A) Remove it and run the engine without it
B) Wash it in petrol and put it back wet
C) Tap it gently or wash foam filters in soapy water and dry completely
D) Blow it with high-pressure air from the inside
quiz.explanation: Cleaning the filter properly restores airflow without damaging it.

quiz.q: Why should you never run a water pump dry?
options: A) It will overheat and damage the seal
B) It will use too much fuel
C) It will make a loud noise
quiz.explanation: Running dry causes friction and heat that destroys the pump seal within minutes.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to clear a jam in a maize mill?
options: B) Switch off, wait for engine to stop, use a wooden stick
C) Keep the engine running and use a metal rod
D) Pour water into the mill
quiz.explanation: Switching off and using a wooden stick prevents serious hand injuries.

quiz.q: When refuelling a machine, you should:
options: A) Do it while the engine is running to save time
B) Smoke a cigarette to keep mosquitoes away
C) Switch off the engine and let it cool
D) Use a plastic bottle as a funnel
quiz.explanation: Fuel vapours can ignite on hot surfaces or sparks, so engine must be off and cool.

quiz.q: What type of fire extinguisher is best for a fuel fire?
quiz.explanation: Dry powder extinguishers are effective on flammable liquid fires.

quiz.q: How can you prevent electric shock from a generator?
options: A) Run it in a wet area
B) Earth the frame with a copper rod
D) Stand in water while operating
quiz.explanation: Earthing the frame safely directs fault currents to the ground.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of cuts when using a circular saw?
quiz.explanation: Dull blades require more force and can slip, causing cuts.

quiz.q: Why should you let a machine cool before touching the exhaust?
quiz.explanation: Exhaust pipes can be hotter than boiling water and cause severe burns.

quiz.q: What should you do with used engine oil?
options: A) Pour it on the ground
B) Use it to light a fire
C) Collect and sell to a recycler
D) Pour it down the drain
quiz.explanation: Proper disposal prevents environmental pollution and can earn a little money.

quiz.q: How long should you let diesel settle before decanting to remove water and dirt?
quiz.explanation: Settling for 24 hours allows contaminants to sink to the bottom.

quiz.q: What is the recommended oil grade for most small Chinese diesels in hot climates?
quiz.explanation: 20W-50 provides better protection at high temperatures.

quiz.q: What should you do if a diesel engine starts then dies immediately?
options: A) Check the fuel cap vent for blockage
C) Add water to the fuel
D) Ignore it and keep trying
quiz.explanation: A blocked fuel cap vent creates a vacuum that stops fuel flow.

quiz.q: What is the correct spark plug gap for most small petrol engines?
quiz.explanation: A gap of 0.7-0.8 mm is standard for small petrol engines.

quiz.q: If a water pump loses prime, what should you check first?
options: A) The suction hose for leaks
B) The colour of the pump
quiz.explanation: Air leaks in the suction hose prevent the pump from drawing water.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a bearing needs replacement?
options: B) It rumbles or makes noise
quiz.explanation: Rumbling indicates worn bearings that can seize if not replaced.

quiz.q: When should you call a professional technician?
options: B) For a clogged air filter
quiz.explanation: Internal engine problems require special tools and expertise.

quiz.q: What should you have ready before a technician arrives?
options: B) Machine model, serial number, and symptoms
quiz.explanation: This information helps the technician diagnose faster.

quiz.q: How often should you grease nipples on a small machine?
quiz.explanation: Regular greasing every 50 hours keeps moving parts lubricated.

quiz.q: What is the danger of using fake lubricants?
options: B) They can ruin your engine
quiz.explanation: Fake oil lacks proper additives and can cause rapid wear.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a logbook for your machine?
options: A) To record hours and maintenance
C) To use as a fire starter
quiz.explanation: A logbook helps track maintenance and predict failures.

quiz.q: What should you do if a machine vibrates excessively?
options: B) Check for worn parts and tighten bolts
quiz.explanation: Vibration often indicates loose or worn components that need attention.

quiz.q: What is the first step if someone gets cut by a machine?
quiz.explanation: Stopping the machine prevents further injury.

quiz.q: How can you prevent slips in the workshop?
options: A) Clean up oil spills immediately
B) Leave tools on the floor
quiz.explanation: Cleaning spills with sand or sawdust prevents slips and falls.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to check if a radiator is hot?
options: A) Touch it with your hand
C) Hold your hand near it without touching
quiz.explanation: Radiating heat can be felt without touching, avoiding burns.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid wearing loose clothing around rotating parts?
options: A) It can get caught and pull you in
quiz.explanation: Loose clothing can be caught by moving parts, causing severe injury.

quiz.q: What should you do before doing any maintenance on a machine?
options: A) Switch off and disconnect power
quiz.explanation: Lockout/tagout prevents accidental start-up during maintenance.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of a clogged fuel filter?
options: B) Engine loses power or stalls
quiz.explanation: A clogged filter restricts fuel flow, causing power loss.

quiz.q: How often should you test the emergency stop button?
quiz.explanation: Weekly testing ensures it works when needed.
